newsitem.title: BULGARIA: BULGARIANS BRACE FOR TOUGH ECONOMIC TIMES.
newsitem.headline: BULGARIANS BRACE FOR TOUGH ECONOMIC TIMES.

text.p: Bulgarians braced for hard times on Friday, with food prices soaring, wages shrinking and petrol supplies cut to a minimum as the Balkan country plunges further into economic chaos.

"We wait two hours for two loaves of bread, then two hours for three cartons of cigarettes, at least we should be able to buy as much as we can afford," an exasperated woman shopper in Sofia told national television.
Bulgaria's pro-market opposition coalition forced the ruling Socialists, the country's ex-communists, to quit on Tuesday and set elections in April -- 20 months ahead of schedule.
Long queues formed outside cigarette shops, where foreign brands were almost impossible to find. Shopkeepers are loathe to buy in dollars and then sell in lev, the national currency.
The plummeting lev was about 2,500 to a dollar on Thursday, compared to about 70 to a dollar a year ago.

The collapsing lev has driven up the cost of petrol imports and only two petrol stations were open in the capital on Thursday. Others around the country were shut or were limiting customers to 20 litres.
Thirty days of popular mass rallies around Bulgaria by the Union of Democratic Forces (UDF) opposition coalition forced the Socialists to quit and call early elections.
Tens of thousands of UDF supporters turned out on Thursday for a victory rally in Plovdiv, the country's second city, to celebrate the fall of the Socialist government.
"Nothing dangerous can happen to us anymore. The worst is behind us," UDF opposition leader Ivan Kostov told the rally.
The UDF has been elected to power only once since 1989 when single-party communist rule fell. The ex-communists reemerged as the Socialists and have retained their grip on power until this week.
The majority Socialists boycotted parliament on Thursday in protest against an agreement to hold an early general election, saying they were being ousted from power by undemocratic means.
President Petar Stoyanov, a pro-reform liberal elected last November, must appoint an interim cabinet to keep the economy afloat and organise the elections.
A presidency spokeswoman said Sofia's respected UDF mayor Stefan Sofianski was a likely candidate for caretaker prime minister.
The UDF, favourite to win the elections after the success of its month-long campaign, must also heal internal rifts and brace itself and its supporters for tough and painful economic reforms.
Bulgaria's students, who suspended daily protests after the Socialists agreed to elections, vowed on Thursday to remain vigilant and insist the country's leaders implement economic reforms.
"After 30 days of protests we have become an important social and political factor. All politicians understand they have to respect us," said student leader Kamen Petrov.
The students won the hearts of many and the contempt of the Socialists with their enthusiastic marches through Sofia.

"Politicians want to use the students ... as the nice young face of their shady political deals", said student leader Avram Stanishev. "We aren't likely to join any campaign but some students are tempted by promises of an easy political career.
